solution: The arrow points to **hydrogen bonds**, the weak bonds that join the base **cytosine (C)** of one strand to **guanine (G)** of the complementary strand. A guanine-cytosine pair is held together by **three hydrogen bonds**, while an adenine-thymine pair has two. These hydrogen bonds hold the two complementary polynucleotide chains of DNA together, while the sugar (S) and phosphate (P) groups form the backbone of each strand.

The building blocks of life are the simple subunits called **monomers** from which the large biomolecules (macromolecules) are built. **Monosaccharides** (simple sugars) are the building blocks of polysaccharides (carbohydrates), **amino acids** are the building blocks of polypeptides (proteins), and **nucleotides** are the building blocks of polynucleotides (nucleic acids). Lipids are formed from **fatty acids** and **glycerol**. All living organisms are chemically built from these same few kinds of subunits.

A **peptide bond** is the bond that links amino acids together in a protein. It joins the **carboxyl group** (\(-\text{COOH}\)) of one amino acid residue to the **amino group** (\(-\text{NH}_2\)) of the next residue, with the removal of a molecule of water, forming a \(-\text{CO}-\text{NH}-\) linkage. Many amino acids joined in this way form a **polypeptide chain**, and a protein consists of one or more such chains. The linear sequence of amino acids held by peptide bonds forms the **primary structure** of a protein.
[Note: the chapter does not state that a water molecule is removed when a peptide bond forms, nor does it give the \(-\text{CO}-\text{NH}-\) group; these are the standard description.]

Polysaccharides are of **two types**:
- **Homopolysaccharides**: polymers of one type of monosaccharide, e.g. **starch** (plant storage molecule), **glycogen** (animal storage molecule) and **cellulose** (cell wall component).
- **Heteropolysaccharides**: polymers of different types of monosaccharides, e.g. **hyaluronic acid**, **heparin**, blood group substances and **chondroitin sulphate**.

By their role, starch and glycogen are reserve (storage) polysaccharides, while cellulose is a structural polysaccharide.

- Carbohydrates **supply energy for metabolism**; they are broken down (oxidised) to release energy.
- **Glucose** is the most important fuel in living cells and the main substrate for **ATP** synthesis.
- **Lactose**, the disaccharide of milk, provides energy to babies fed on milk.
- **Starch** in plants and **glycogen** in animals (in the liver and muscles) are stored as **reserve food** and are hydrolysed to glucose as needed.
- Polysaccharides are **structural components**: **cellulose** forms the tough cell walls of plant cells, and polysaccharides are also components of the cell membrane.
- The pentose sugars **ribose** and **deoxyribose** form part of RNA and DNA respectively.

A **reducing sugar** is a sugar that has a **free aldehyde** (\(-\text{CHO}\)) **or ketone** (\(\text{C}=\text{O}\)) **group** and can therefore reduce **Benedict's reagent**, changing \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) to \(\text{Cu}^{+}\). It does this by transferring hydrogens (electrons) to the other compound. All monosaccharides, such as glucose and fructose, are reducing sugars, and so are the disaccharides **lactose** and **maltose**. **Sucrose** is a non-reducing sugar because it lacks a free aldehyde or ketone group.

A **saturated fatty acid** has **no double bonds** between the carbon atoms of its hydrocarbon chain, e.g. **palmitic acid** and **stearic acid**. An **unsaturated fatty acid** has **one or more double bonds** between the carbon atoms of its hydrocarbon chain, e.g. **oleic acid** and **linoleic acid**. Fats rich in unsaturated fatty acids are generally liquid at room temperature and are called oils; unsaturated fatty acids can be hydrogenated to produce solid fats such as vanaspati ghee.

**Simple proteins** are proteins that yield only amino acids on hydrolysis. Examples:
- **Histones**: soluble in water; their globular molecules are not coagulated by heat. They are **basic proteins**, rich in lysine and arginine. **Significance:** histones are coupled with nucleic acids to form **nucleoproteins**.
- **Albumins**: soluble in water but coagulated on heating, and widely distributed, e.g. **egg albumin**, **serum albumin** and **legumelin** of pulses. **Significance:** egg albumin and legumelin are food (nutritive) proteins, and serum albumin of blood plasma maintains the osmotic pressure of blood and carries substances in it.
[Note: the chapter does not state the functions of albumins; their nutritive role and the osmotic and carrier role of serum albumin are the standard description.]

The **secondary structure** of a protein is the regular coiling or folding of its polypeptide chain, held together by **hydrogen bonds**. The sequence of amino acids decides where the chain bends or folds and where hydrogen bonds form, either between different portions of the same chain or between different chains. It occurs in two forms:
- **α-helix**: the polypeptide chain is coiled like a right-handed spiral, held by hydrogen bonds within the chain, e.g. **keratin** of hair.
- **β-pleated sheet**: two or more peptide chains lie side by side and are linked by intermolecular hydrogen bonds, forming a pleated sheet, e.g. the protein of **silk fibres**.
[Note: the textbook says that left-handed spirals are called the β-helix; the second form of secondary structure is the β-pleated sheet (the chapter's 'pleated sheet'), a sheet of extended chains rather than a helix.]

The **induced fit model** (flexible model) was proposed by **Koshland**. It states that the approach of a substrate **induces a conformational change** in the enzyme. The enzyme is not a rigid structure, as in Fischer's lock and key model, but a **flexible** one: its **active site** continually reshapes by interacting with the substrate until the substrate is completely bound to it, and at that point the final form and shape of the enzyme is determined. The enzyme-substrate complex so formed changes the distribution of electrons in the chemical bonds of the substrate, which leads to the formation of products. The products are then released and the enzyme is regenerated for another reaction cycle. The induced fit model is the more accepted model of the mode of enzyme action (Fig. 6.18).

**RNA (ribonucleic acid)** is a nucleic acid made of a polynucleotide chain, usually **single stranded**, whose nucleotides contain **ribose** sugar instead of deoxyribose, and **uracil** in place of thymine. In most organisms it is not the hereditary material, but in some, such as **tobacco mosaic virus**, it is. In a few cases, e.g. reovirus and wound tumour virus, RNA is double stranded.

The three types of cellular RNA are:
1. **Messenger RNA (mRNA)** or template RNA
2. **Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)**
3. **Transfer RNA (tRNA)** or soluble RNA

The **metabolic pool** is the reservoir of biomolecules in the cell on which enzymes can act to produce useful products as per the need of the cell. Catabolic reactions such as **glycolysis** and the **Krebs cycle** not only provide ATP but also make available a pool of biomolecules that can be used to synthesise many important cellular components. Metabolites can be **added to or withdrawn from** this pool according to the need of the cell. The concept is significant because it allows one type of molecule to change into another, e.g. **carbohydrates can be converted to fats and vice versa**. The balance between catabolism and anabolism maintains homeostasis in the cell as well as in the whole body.

**Secondary metabolites** are small organic molecules produced by bacteria, fungi and plants that are not essential for their growth, development and reproduction, but they are useful to mankind in many ways:
- **Medicines**: drugs developed from secondary metabolites are used to treat infectious diseases, cancer, hypertension and inflammation.
- **Morphine**, the first alkaloid isolated from *Papaver somniferum*, is used as a pain reliever and cough suppressant.
- **Flavours**: secondary metabolites give food its flavours and improve our food preferences, e.g. the flavour and aroma of cabbage come from **glucosinolates**.
- **Tannins** are added to wines and chocolate to improve their astringency.
- **Food preservatives**: since most secondary metabolites have antibiotic properties, they are used as food preservatives.

**Biomolecules** are the chemical molecules present in the protoplasm of the cells of living organisms. Chemical analysis of living tissue shows elements such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, calcium, phosphorus and magnesium. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are the **prime elements**; nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur are **macro elements**; boron, chlorine, zinc, copper, iron, sodium, molybdenum, nickel, silicon and cobalt are **trace elements**.

Biomolecules are **inorganic** or **organic**. Organic biomolecules are of two kinds:
- **Macromolecules**: the large polymers **polysaccharides** (carbohydrates), **polypeptides** (proteins) and **polynucleotides** (nucleic acids).
- **Micromolecules**: small molecules such as simple sugars, amino acids, nucleotides, lipids and secondary metabolites.

**Building blocks of life:** every macromolecule is a polymer of simple subunits called **monomers**. **Monosaccharides** (simple sugars) are the building blocks of polysaccharides, **amino acids** of polypeptides, and **nucleotides** of polynucleotides. Lipids, which are water insoluble and of small molecular weight compared with macromolecules, are made from **fatty acids** (saturated and unsaturated) and **glycerol**. The monomers join together to form the macromolecules; for example, monosaccharides join by condensation reactions to form polysaccharides, which are broken down again into monosaccharides by hydrolysis (Fig. 6.1).

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with the general formula \(\text{C}_x(\text{H}_2\text{O})_y\). Based on the number of sugar units they are classified into three classes:

1. **Monosaccharides** (simple sugars): the simplest sugars, crystalline, sweet and soluble in water, which cannot be hydrolysed further. Their general formula is \((\text{CH}_2\text{O})_n\), where n is 3 to 7. By the number of carbon atoms they are trioses (glyceraldehyde), tetroses (erythrose), pentoses (ribose in RNA, deoxyribose in DNA), hexoses (glucose, fructose, galactose) and heptoses (sedoheptulose). Those with an aldehyde group are **aldoses** (glucose, xylose) and those with a ketone group are **ketoses** (ribulose, fructose).
2. **Disaccharides**: formed when two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction releasing a water molecule; the two units are held by a **glycosidic bond**. Examples: **sucrose** (cane sugar), which gives glucose and fructose on hydrolysis; **lactose** (milk sugar), which gives glucose and galactose; **maltose** (malt sugar), which gives two glucose units. Sucrose is non-reducing, while lactose and maltose are reducing sugars.
3. **Polysaccharides**: very large molecules formed by polymerization of monosaccharides. **Homopolysaccharides** are polymers of one type of monosaccharide, e.g. **starch** (plant reserve, as amylose and amylopectin), **glycogen** (animal reserve in liver and muscles) and **cellulose** (plant cell walls, made of β-glucose). **Heteropolysaccharides** are polymers of different monosaccharides, e.g. hyaluronic acid, heparin, blood group substances and chondroitin sulphate.

**Lipids** are greasy substances with long hydrocarbon chains made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, soluble in organic (non-polar) solvents; they are fatty acids and their derivatives. They are of three types:

1. **Simple lipids**: esters of fatty acids with various alcohols.
   - **Fats** (triglycerides) are esters of three fatty acid molecules with one molecule of glycerol (\(\text{CH}_2\text{OH}-\text{CHOH}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)). Unsaturated fats liquid at room temperature are called oils. **Significance:** fats are reserve food of high calorific value; in plants they are stored in seeds to nourish the embryo during germination, and in animals in the adipocytes of adipose tissue. Subcutaneous fat acts as an insulator that minimises loss of body heat, and fat around internal organs acts as a cushion against mechanical shocks.
   - **Waxes** are esters of long chain fatty acids with long chain alcohols, solid at ordinary temperature, e.g. wax of the beehive. **Significance:** they form a water insoluble coating on the hair and skin of animals and on the stems, leaves and fruits of plants.
2. **Compound lipids**: esters of fatty acids carrying other groups. **Phospholipids** contain a phosphate group (lecithin also has a nitrogenous compound) and form the **cell membrane**. **Glycolipids** contain a simple sugar such as galactose; the cerebrosides among them occur in large amounts in the white matter of the brain and the myelin sheath.
3. **Derived lipids**: **sterols**, made of fused hydrocarbon rings (steroid nucleus) with a long side chain. **Cholesterol** occurs in all animal cells, particularly nervous tissue; adrenocorticoids, sex hormones (progesterone, testosterone) and vitamin D are synthesised from it. Plants have **phytosterols**; the yam plant (*Dioscorea*) produces **diosgenin**, used to make anti-fertility pills.
[Note: the textbook says glycolipids contain glycerol and calls all of them cerebrosides; cerebrosides are built on sphingosine rather than glycerol.]

**Chemical nature:** phospholipids are **compound lipids**, esters of fatty acids that carry a **phosphate group**. A phospholipid molecule contains one molecule of **glycerol**, **two molecules of fatty acids** and a **phosphate group**. In some phospholipids, such as **lecithin**, a nitrogenous compound is also attached to the phosphate group.

**Structure:** a phospholipid molecule has two distinct parts:
- a **polar head** (the phosphate and nitrogenous group), which is **hydrophilic** (water loving);
- two **non-polar tails** (the hydrocarbon chains of the fatty acids), which are **hydrophobic** (water repelling).

**Role in the biological membrane:** phospholipids form the cell membrane. In an aqueous medium they arrange themselves as a **lipid bilayer** (Fig. 6.9): the polar heads of the two layers face the water on either side, and the non-polar tails point inwards, towards each other, away from the water. This bilayer is the basic structure of the cell membrane that separates the cell from its watery surroundings.

Proteins are large molecules of 100 to 3000 amino acid units joined by peptide bonds. On the basis of structure they are classified into three classes:

1. **Simple proteins**: yield only amino acids on hydrolysis.
   - **Histones**: water soluble, not coagulated by heat; basic proteins that combine with nucleic acids to form **nucleoproteins**.
   - **Albumins**: water soluble but coagulated on heating, e.g. egg albumin, serum albumin and legumelin of pulses.
2. **Conjugated proteins**: a simple protein united with a non-protein substance called the **prosthetic group**.
   - **Haemoglobin**: the protein globin with the iron containing pigment haem; it plays an indispensable part in respiration.
   - **Nucleoproteins**: nucleic acids coupled with histone proteins.
   - **Mucoproteins** (glycoproteins): carbohydrate-protein complexes, e.g. **mucin** of saliva.
   - **Lipoproteins**: lipid-protein complexes found in the brain, the plasma membrane, milk etc.
3. **Derived proteins**: not found in nature as such but derived from native proteins on hydrolysis, e.g. **metaproteins** and **peptones**.

**Importance:** proteins are of primary importance to the cell; almost all enzymes are proteins, structural proteins such as **keratin** form hair, haemoglobin works in respiration, and nucleoproteins carry the nucleic acids.
[Note: the textbook also gives heparin of blood as a mucoprotein; heparin is a heteropolysaccharide, as the chapter's own Table 6.2 lists it.]

**Enzymes** are biocatalysts: substances made by living cells that speed up the chemical reactions of the cell at body temperature while remaining unchanged themselves. All enzymes are proteins except ribozymes. Without enzymes, the reactions of the cell would either not occur or occur very slowly.

Enzymes are classified into six classes according to the type of reaction they catalyse:

1. **Oxidoreductases**: catalyse oxidation and reduction by transfer of hydrogen and/or oxygen, e.g. **alcohol dehydrogenase**: \(\text{Alcohol} + \text{NAD}^+ \rightarrow \text{Aldehyde} + \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\)
2. **Transferases**: catalyse the transfer of certain groups between two molecules, e.g. **glucokinase**: \(\text{Glucose} + \text{ATP} \rightarrow \text{Glucose-6-phosphate} + \text{ADP}\)
3. **Hydrolases**: catalyse hydrolytic reactions, e.g. amylases, proteases, lipases and **sucrase**: \(\text{Sucrose} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Glucose} + \text{Fructose}\)
4. **Lyases**: remove a group of atoms from the substrate leaving a double bond, e.g. aldolases, decarboxylases, dehydratases, fumarate hydratase and **histidine decarboxylase**: \(\text{Histidine} \rightarrow \text{Histamine} + \text{CO}_2\)
5. **Isomerases**: catalyse structural rearrangements within a molecule, e.g. xylose isomerase and **glucose-6-phosphate isomerase**: \(\text{Glucose-6-phosphate} \rightarrow \text{Fructose-6-phosphate}\)
6. **Ligases (synthetases)**: catalyse the covalent linkage of molecules using energy from ATP or GTP, e.g. glutathione synthetase and **pyruvate carboxylase**: \(\text{Pyruvate} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{ATP} \rightarrow \text{Oxaloacetate} + \text{ADP} + \text{P}_i\)

1. **Proteinaceous nature**: all enzymes are basically made of protein, except ribozymes. Some are purely protein (e.g. proteases); others are conjugated enzymes with a non-protein **prosthetic group**, and the protein part (**apoenzyme**) with the prosthetic group forms the **holoenzyme**. Some enzymes need co-enzymes (e.g. NAD, FMN) or metal ion co-factors (e.g. iron for catalase).
2. **Three-dimensional conformation**: every enzyme has a specific 3-D shape with one or more **active sites** where the substrate binds.
3. **Catalytic property**: enzymes speed up biochemical reactions but remain unchanged, so after releasing the product they can catalyse the reaction again. A small quantity of enzyme acts on a very large quantity of substrate; sucrase can hydrolyse about 100000 times its own weight of sucrose.
4. **Specificity of action**: each enzyme acts on a specific substrate or group of substrates and catalyses one specific reaction; this is its most significant property.
5. **Sensitivity to pH**: each enzyme works best at its **optimum pH**, e.g. pepsin at pH 2 (acidic) and trypsin at pH 9.5 (alkaline).
6. **Sensitivity to temperature**: enzymes are destroyed (denatured) at high temperatures of 60-70°C and become temporarily inactive below 4°C; most work best between 20°C and 35°C.
7. **Activity outside the cell**: enzymes retain their catalytic property even when extracted from cells; they may act inside the cell (endo-enzymes) or outside it (exo-enzymes, e.g. those released by fungi).

1. **Concentration of substrate**: increasing the substrate concentration gradually increases the velocity of the reaction, but only within a limited range; the velocity then levels off at a maximum (\(V_{max}\)), so the plot of velocity against substrate concentration is a **rectangular hyperbola**. The **Michaelis-Menten constant (\(K_m\))** is the substrate concentration that gives half the maximum velocity; a low \(K_m\) shows strong affinity of the enzyme for its substrate, and a high \(K_m\) weak affinity.
2. **Concentration of enzyme**: when enough substrate is present, the rate of reaction increases with increasing enzyme concentration and decreases when the enzyme concentration is lowered.
3. **Temperature**: the rate rises with temperature only over a limited range. Enzymatic reactions occur best at the **optimum temperature**, about 37°C (normal body temperature) in homeotherms. Activity is reduced at low temperature, and at high temperature enzymes are denatured.
4. **pH**: each enzyme works at its maximum rate at its own **optimum pH** and cannot function beyond its pH range, e.g. pepsin at pH 2 and trypsin at pH 9.5.
5. **Other substances**: **co-enzymes** and **activators** (inorganic substances) increase enzyme activity, while **inhibitors** retard it.
[Note: the textbook says the rate of reaction is directly proportional to the substrate concentration and to the square root of the enzyme concentration; the rate rises with substrate concentration only until the enzyme approaches saturation, and with substrate in excess it is directly proportional to the enzyme concentration. The chapter also gives two figures for denaturation, above 40°C and at 60-70°C.]

**Nucleic acids** are polynucleotides, among the largest molecules found in living beings. Each is a long chain of **nucleotides**, and each nucleotide is made of three molecules: a **5-carbon (pentose) sugar**, **phosphoric acid** and a **nitrogen containing base**. They were first isolated from pus cells by Friedrich Miescher, and are of two types, DNA and RNA.

| Point | DNA | RNA |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar | Deoxyribose | Ribose |
| Bases | Adenine, guanine, cytosine and **thymine** | Adenine, guanine, cytosine and **uracil** |
| Strands | Usually two strands twisted into a **double helix** (single stranded in bacteriophage \(\phi\)X174) | Usually a **single strand**, folded on itself (double stranded in reovirus) |
| Base equality | Purines equal pyrimidines (A = T, G = C) | No purine-pyrimidine equality |
| Role | Hereditary material in most organisms | Hereditary material only in some, e.g. tobacco mosaic virus |
| Types | One type | Three types: mRNA, rRNA and tRNA |

There are three types of cellular RNA:

1. **Messenger RNA (mRNA)** or template RNA: a linear polynucleotide that forms about 3% of the total cellular RNA. **Role:** it carries the **genetic information** for arranging amino acids in a definite sequence. An mRNA carrying the information for one complete polypeptide chain is called a **cistron**, and the size of an mRNA depends on the size of the message it carries.
2. **Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)**: forms 80-90% of the cellular RNA and is synthesised in the nucleus; it is coiled here and there by complementary base pairing within the chain. **Role:** it forms 50-60% of the **ribosomes**, being a structural part of them.
3. **Transfer RNA (tRNA)** or soluble RNA: small molecules of 70-80 nucleotides, folded into a **clover-leaf** shape. **Role:** each tRNA picks up a **particular amino acid**, which is attached at the 3' end in its acceptor stem. Its anticodon loop carries three unpaired nucleotides, the **anticodon**, which pair with the complementary **codon** on mRNA. It also has the DHU arm (dihydrouridine loop) and a ribosome recognition site.
[Note: the textbook spells the DHU arm 'dihydroxyuridine'; the D in DHU stands for dihydrouridine.]

**Metabolism** is the sum of the chemical reactions that take place within each cell of a living organism, providing energy for vital processes and for synthesising new organic material. It is a continuous process of breakdown and synthesis of biomolecules, and its reactions are always linked with other reactions. It has two types of pathways:
- **Catabolic pathways** break complex biomolecules into simpler ones and release energy as ATP, e.g. digestion of the starch of wheat or chapati to glucose.
- **Anabolic (biosynthetic) pathways** build complex biomolecules from simpler ones and consume energy, e.g. synthesis of glycogen from glucose and of proteins from amino acids.

**Formation of the metabolic pool:** in catabolism, carbohydrates (glycogen, starch) are broken down to **glucose**, lipids (triglycerides) to **glycerol and fatty acids**, and proteins to **amino acids** (Fig. 6.22). The catabolic reactions of **glycolysis** and the **Krebs cycle** not only provide ATP but also make these biomolecules available in a common reservoir, the **metabolic pool**. Enzymes act on this pool to produce useful products as the cell needs them: metabolites are added to it or withdrawn from it for the synthesis of cellular components. Because all these molecules meet in one pool, one type can change into another, e.g. carbohydrates into fats and vice versa. The balance between catabolism and anabolism maintains homeostasis in the cell and the whole body.

In double stranded DNA, guanine always pairs with cytosine and adenine with thymine, so the amount of G equals the amount of C and the amount of A equals the amount of T (Chargaff's rule).

- Cytosine (C) = 14%, so **guanine (G) = 14%**.
- C + G = 14% + 14% = 28%.
- A + T = 100% - 28% = 72%, and since A = T, each is 72% / 2 = 36%.

Therefore, **adenine (A) = 36%**, **thymine (T) = 36%** and **guanine (G) = 14%**.
**Metabolism**. It is the sum of all the chemical reactions, both catabolic (breakdown) and anabolic (synthesis), that take place within the cells of a living organism.

**Sucrose**. This disaccharide of glucose and fructose is the form in which carbohydrate made in the leaves is transported through the plant.
[Note: the chapter does not state the form in which carbohydrate is transported in plants; sucrose is the standard answer.]
**Benedict's reagent**. Reducing sugars, which have a free aldehyde or ketone group, reduce the \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) of Benedict's reagent to \(\text{Cu}^{+}\).
